items.original_title: No Perfect Route: Building Supply Chain Resilience Across China and Southeast Asia
items.summary: Summary: New Statista research and expert insight on what it takes to build real-world supply chain flexibility. When was the last time your logistics plan actually went to plan? In logistics, disruption is expected. More options, more routes, but not more resilience Last year, trade between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) exceeded US$1.05 trillion. The real resilience builder: systems, data, partners and handovers that make full use of the route options Transporting freight from China through Southeast Asia can involve a long chain of organisations: freight forwarders, trucking companies, terminals, customs agencies, brokers, ports, airlines, shipping lines and warehouses might all touch the same shipment. Research conducted with 260 logistics and supply chain decision-makers across Asia-Pacific found that organisations differ significantly in their ability to anticipate, absorb and respond to disruption. To help organisations evaluate their readiness, No Perfect Route introduces a Supply Chain Resilience Maturity Model that identifies five stages of resilience capability, from reactive response to proactive orchestration. Stage 3: Connected Systems exchange data across supply chain partners, but execution relies on checkpoint updates rather than real-time tracking. Stage 4: Orchestrated Alternative routes are pre-costed, pre-tested, and backed by pre-approved decision rights.

items.summary: A comprehensive new report entitled Securing Trust: The Transition to Digital Seafarer Credentials, published by maritime technology research firm Thetius in partnership with Maritime Passport, reveals that the global shipping industry’s reliance on paper certificates and disconnected digital copies poses significant operational, security, and administrative risks. With an estimated 2.57 million seafarers serving on more than 85,000 merchant ships worldwide, maritime professionals are still routinely required to carry physical copies of certificates weighing up to four kilograms. The report emphasises that simply converting physical documents into unstructured electronic PDFs or disconnected digital portals cannot solve the industry’s verification challenge. “As an ex-seafarer myself, I have long been advocating for greater use of digital technologies in ways that benefit seafarers, and this report highlights the ways in which digital verification can and must evolve. Digital credentials must reinforce issuing authority while giving employers, inspectors, and other key stakeholders confidence that every credential is valid, up to date, and held by the rightful individual.” Key findings of the Report Heavy administrative burden: Verifying credentials for a single seafarer can take between one and two hours for crewing recruitment teams. Scanned copies and PDFs do not fix this: credentials need to be linked to verified digital identities that can be checked independently.

In findings released Tuesday, the NTSB issued six safety recommendations addressing vessel visibility, collision avoidance, and remote monitoring, highlighting regulatory gaps as uncrewed and autonomous vessels become increasingly common in U.S. The investigation stems from an August 10, 2024, collision between a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) SeaTrac SP-48 uncrewed surface vessel and a privately owned 45-foot Prestige 450 Flybridge recreational boat approximately six miles east-southeast of Monroe, Michigan. According to the NTSB investigation report, the uncrewed vessel’s low-profile design made it particularly difficult for other mariners to see. The agency also issued three recommendations to NOAA, calling for revisions to its internal operating procedures to ensure its uncrewed vessels can be adequately detected by other mariners. The recommendations come as the maritime industry increasingly adopts uncrewed vessels for oceanographic research, hydrographic surveying, environmental monitoring, and other operations.

items.title: Russia Ships Less Crude Even as Key Baltic Port’s Flows Rebound
items.original_title: Russia Ships Less Crude Even as Key Baltic Port’s Flows Rebound
items.summary: Fuga Bluemarine crude oil tanker lies at anchor near the terminal Kozmino in Nakhodka Bay near the port city of Nakhodka, Russia, December 4, 2022. REUTERS/Tatiana Meel (Bloomberg) — Russia shipped the least crude in more than a month, even as operations at its key Baltic port recovered strongly from an earlier halt. In the four weeks through Oct. 25, overseas crude flows edged lower to 3.55 million barrels a day, tanker data compiled by Bloomberg showed. The shift comes as crude flows from the Middle East return to near pre-war levels. The small drop in total flows and lower prices for Russia’s key Urals crude were offset by higher prices for the Pacific ESPO grade. Ships still showing their destinations as their Russian loading ports, or places such as Gibraltar, are recorded as “Other Unknown.” Observed shipments to Russia’s Asian customers, including those showing no final destination, edged lower to to 3.42 million barrels a day in the 28 days to Oct. An earlier flurry of shipments to Egypt, which took flows to as much as 160,000 barrels a day in mid-June, has fallen back to about 50,000 barrels a day in the most recent period.

items.summary: The Pier 300 channel at the Port of Los Angeles. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles A labor dispute involving port watchmen could disrupt operations at eight marine terminals in the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach as early as November 1, just weeks after the nation’s busiest container port complex reported record cargo volumes. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 has warned fellow maritime unions that its members may go on strike when the latest extension of their labor agreement expires on Sunday. The eight affected terminal locations are APM Terminals (APMT), Long Beach Container Terminal (LBCT), Total Terminals International (TTI), SSA at C-60, A-90, LB 206, Pacific Container Terminal (PCT), and OH 55. Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September , handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting global trade patterns drove cargo through the complex. The PMA was also at the center of the last major West Coast port labor dispute in 2023, when contentious negotiations with the ILWU led to work slowdowns and terminal shutdowns at several ports, including Los Angeles and Long Beach.

Ahead of Champi’s arrival, Taiwan’s key ports Kaohsiung, Taipei and Keelung closed last Friday and resumed operations over the weekend. These disruptions are temporarily absorbing effective capacity and offering some support to spot rates.” Nevertheless, the underlying supply-demand imbalance remains unresolved, leaving carriers struggling to sustain pricing ahead of their planned 1 November GRI. items.summary: Shippers are scrambling to make alternative arrangement for inland container movements in the UK after a train derailment forced the suspension of rail services to key terminals in the south-east, including DP World London Gateway. A spokesperson for DP World told The Loadstar : “We are currently operating a reduced rail freight service from our London Gateway terminal. We are working closely with customers and with Network Rail to minimise disruption while repairs to the network are carried out.” Hapag-Lloyd has warned customers that inland cargo movements were likely to be impacted, advising them to arrange road transport for any containers booked under merchant haulage arrangements. For customers using carrier haulage, the German liner noted that its inland team would discuss alternative transport arrangements, but warned it would be unable to accept additional haulage requests during the disruption. Whether there is sufficient trucking capacity to absorb the displaced rail volumes remains unclear, but as with much of the world, the UK’s haulage industry has been contending with a decades-long crisis in attracting new talent.

items.title: Tariff anouncements cause cargo chaos for box terminals, says TiL
items.original_title: Tariff anouncements cause cargo chaos for box terminals, says TiL
items.summary: Sudden tariff announcements, not tariff levels themselves, trigger costly cargo surges that terminals cannot absorb, delegates at TOC Americas in Cartagena were told. Rather than destroying container trade, said TiL Group’s director for terminal investments in North America, Tom van Eynde, tariffs were relocating it, pointing to cargo shifting from Canadian ports into TiL’s US terminals as evidence. “It has been somewhat of a wild ride over the past year, the past two years,” Mr van Eynde noted, referring to tariffs in the US being introduced and then cancelled. “They’re not really reducing the trade flows, they’re just relocating them.” While the terminal operator saw a reduction in certain trade flows to the US through Canadian ports, he said these were then automatically being picked up by TiL terminals in US ports. Expecting the situation to be “a temporary thing”, Mr van Eynde said he expected disruption to settle once tariffs hit a range of 10% to 15% – “at that kind of level we see very little impact anymore on the volume.” The real damage, he said, came less from the tariffs themselves than from sudden announcements that triggered a rush of cargo before a deadline, only for conditions to return to normal once it passed.

The war led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, preventing Qatar, which holds about 19% of global LNG market share as the world’s second-largest exporter, from shipping most cargoes to Asian and European buyers. China, the world’s largest importer of the super-chilled fuel, is driving the October increase. Kpler projects Chinese arrivals of 5.47 million tons, up from 5.20 million in September, making it the third-strongest month in 2026. The uptick in Chinese purchases suggests demand ahead of the northern winter is outweighing price concerns. Spot LNG for delivery to north Asia reached $29.30 per million British thermal units in the week to October 16, the highest since December 2023 and nearly triple the $10.40 level from late February before the Iran conflict started.

items.title: New study pours cold water on nuclear shipping economics
items.original_title: New study pours cold water on nuclear shipping economics
items.summary: The commercial case for nuclear-powered shipping remains highly uncertain, with new research suggesting the technology could become competitive by 2040, but only with dramatic reductions in reactor costs and effective global carbon regulation. A study published today by University College London’s Energy Institute examines the total cost of ownership of nuclear-powered containerships, comparing them with conventionally fuelled and ammonia-powered alternatives. A conventional containership costs $119.6m in the model, compared with $148.5m for an ammonia dual-fuel vessel. The nuclear equivalent ranges from $228m under optimistic assumptions to $582m for first-of-a-kind reactor technology. The researchers calculate that reactor production costs would need to fall by as much as 80% for nuclear propulsion to become commercially attractive, reductions that have yet to be demonstrated. Under the most favourable assumptions, nuclear becomes the cheapest propulsion option from 2040, but only when the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework is included, allowing nuclear vessels to earn revenue from surplus emissions credits. The study also challenges the argument that nuclear propulsion could transform container shipping economics by allowing vessels to travel considerably faster. The central question is who will finance the expensive first generation of nuclear ships before the economies of scale needed to make the technology competitive materialise.

NYK and K Line will establish an equally owned joint venture to market and supply the fuel, primarily through ship-to-ship bunkering at Nagoya and Mikawa. The partners describe the initiative as the world’s first integrated commercial ammonia marine fuel supply chain linking procurement, bunkering infrastructure and vessel operations. The new car carriers will incorporate multiple layers of protection against ammonia leaks, including detection and neutralisation systems, reflecting the fuel’s toxicity and corrosiveness. The announcement follows Japan’s first ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering operation to an ammonia-fuelled vessel in September, led by NYK.

It was designed to set global shipping on a course to net-zero by 2050 in a just and equitable way. Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually, roughly as much as the economies of Germany or Japan. While T&E analysis has previously shown that the NZF in itself is not strong enough to reduce shipping emissions at the pace countries agreed to, the agreement set an important global standard for a sector so far exempt from most climate rules. The EU is clear that if the IMO establishes a carbon pricing scheme such as the NZF, a ship sailing internationally will not have to pay double for the same emissions under the EU ETS. The newly proposed “ETS as a service” would allow EU trade partners to raise revenues on their own 50% shares through the EU’s existing system, without the administrative burden of setting up their own ETS from scratch. Now, the EU is opening a path for its regional rules to co-exist with a global framework and involving others in the benefits.

items.title: Congestion-induced ‘double sailings’ cancel out Golden Week blanks
items.original_title: Congestion-induced ‘double sailings’ cancel out Golden Week blanks
items.summary: Deployed capacity on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades during this year’s Golden Week holiday was the highest on record, according to new analysis from Sea-Intelligence. Port congestion in Asia, caused by a succession of typhoons, led to vessel bunching at loading ports, and subsequently resulted in a series of “double sailings”, which cancelled out carriers’ blanking strategy during the holiday period when they typically look to skip voyages due to a lack of cargo sitting on Asia’s docks “Double sailings are essentially two departures on a liner service in a week,” analysts at Sea-Intelligence said. “Liner services work on weekly departure frequencies – ie, one vessel departs the origin region every week. “When vessels get delayed, they bunch up – the delayed departure that moved from week 1 to week 2 is now sailing along with the original week 2 departure, hence a ‘double sailing’,” the consultancy explained. This meant deployed capacity during the Golden Week period – which Sea-Intelligence defined as taking place between weeks 40 and 42, to account for the lag in inland transport work unable to take place because drivers were on holiday – was this year higher on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades than ever before.

For example, Indian importers are now able to book a 40ft shipment from Shanghai to JNPA at about $3,200 per box, down from about $3,800 a month ago. Hong Kong-JNPA rates are currently in the region of $3,600/40ft, down from $3,800 a month ago, while carriers are booking freight from Singapore to JNPA at about $3,400/40ft, 5% lower than in September. Spot rates from Hong Kong to Chennai have fallen 15%, to $3,300/40ft, the data indicates. But executives at leading intra-Asia carriers claimed the latest moderate correction should not be seen as the onset of a broader cyclical downturn as, according to them, trades from Asia to India and the Middle East still remained caught up in port challenges and delays across the region. “Our Asia-India-Middle East vessels continue to operate under a lot of operational strain on the Persian Gulf end,” one source told The Loadstar.

The additional reservations will be offered at the authority’s discretion, depending on operational capacity and availability. The easing comes after the canal closed its 2026 financial year with record cargo tonnage. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the 12 months to September 30, up 4.1% year on year, while tonnage increased 6.5% to 521m Panama Canal measurement tons. Neopanamax traffic accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with volumes through the larger locks rising 8.2% compared with the previous financial year. The canal has also been expanding its longer-term reservation arrangements. That programme will cover January 3 to April 3, 2027, providing 288 Panamax slots alongside 270 neopanamax slots through competitive allocations in November. From January 3, 2027, booking swaps and substitutions between shipping alliance members will be extended to vessels in the panamax super category, arrangements previously available only to neopanamax ships.

items.summary: Europe’s carbon market could soon start paying shipowners to switch fuels, but the support on offer is far from equal. In July, the European Commission proposed a revision of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) that would reserve up to 110 million allowances between 2028 and 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, which is meant to cover part of the price gap between fossil marine fuels and sustainable alternatives. Rystad Energy’s analysis shows that, combined with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would reshape the cost ranking of marine fuels in Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels stand to gain the most, while biodiesel made from used cooking oil (UCO) and animal fats – one of today’s most widely used marine biofuels – is left out. SMAP would cover 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with 10 additional percentage points where the feedstock is sourced in the EU. At 3Q26 prices, bioLNG costs more than twice as much as VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at about half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are counted.

items.title: Trump Administration Unveils Seafood Strategy to Boost U.S. Fishing Fleet and Domestic Production
items.original_title: Trump Administration Unveils Seafood Strategy to Boost U.S. Fishing Fleet and Domestic Production
items.summary: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure, and tougher enforcement against unfair foreign competition. The strategy , announced October 23, builds on President Donald Trump’s April 2025 executive order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness , and brings together several federal agencies to expand domestic seafood production, modernize processing capacity, and improve market access for American fishermen. The initiative comes as the administration pursues a broader effort to rebuild America’s maritime industrial base, including domestic shipbuilding capacity and the U.S.-flagged fleet. The administration also plans to strengthen the position of American seafood in domestic markets. Trade Representative will also work with other agencies to address unfair foreign trade practices and improve access to overseas markets for American seafood exporters. NOAA said progress will be measured through increases in domestic seafood production and processing, private capital investment, American jobs supported, and reduced dependence on foreign supply chains. The broader goal is to keep more of the economic value of American seafood in the United States, from vessels harvesting fish offshore to the shipyards, processors, and waterfront businesses that support the industry.

Tariffs on China’s Russian oil purchases could reignite trade tensions with the US while doing little to deter such purchases, given the economic appeal of discounted Russian crude for Chinese refiners.

items.title: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading
items.original_title: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading
items.summary: In the briefing, authors Daniel Martin, HFW partner, and Amanda Rathbone, HFW knowledge counsel (commodities) said that sanctions compliance has evolved from a specialist legal consideration into a central strategic concern for commodity businesses trading oil, gas, metals and agricultural products. Martin and Rathbone warn that the sanctions environment is changing so rapidly that risks can evolve significantly during the lifecycle of a single transaction, from initial negotiations through to shipment, financing and payment. As a result, companies are increasingly being forced to reassess traditional compliance processes and adopt broader, more dynamic risk management strategies. Governments are increasingly using sanctions as instruments of broader geopolitical policy, meaning that ordinary commercial activity and seemingly routine commodity trades can now attract scrutiny. HFW warns that efforts to comply with one jurisdiction’s sanctions requirements can sometimes increase exposure to conflicting regulations elsewhere, creating difficult commercial and legal dilemmas for international trading businesses. The briefing also points to increasing expectations from regulators, who now expect companies to investigate broader sanctions risks throughout a transaction rather than relying solely on screening immediate contractual counterparties against sanctions lists. Martin and Rathbone believe sanctions complexity is unlikely to diminish.

items.original_title: Seafarers face widening competency gap as digital shipping accelerates, recent research finds
items.summary: Eighty two per cent of maritime professionals surveyed say current training does not adequately prepare crews for the realities of modern, digitally-enabled vessel operations. Seafarer training is falling behind rapidly evolving operational realities at sea, according to two new reports commissioned by OneOcean and conducted by maritime innovation consultancy Thetius. Findings reveal two interconnected challenges – that seafarers work in increasingly complex digital environments, and that maritime professionals do not feel well prepared to keep pace with this change. Alex Mangan, Chief Marketing and Communications Officer, OneOcean, said: “Change in shipping will only accelerate as vessels adopt new digital systems to manage tightening international regulation and to sail more efficiently and productively. “This has created a growing gap between the training seafarers receive and the challenges they face at sea. Closing this reality gap requires the industry to shift its approaches to competence, to reflect real-world operations.” Nick Chubb, Founder of Thetius, said: “The findings reveal a clear reality gap between the demands of modern shipping and the way competence is developed. As vessels become more digitally complex, the industry must move beyond compliance-based training and equip seafarers with the skills they need to operate safely and effectively.” OneOcean’s own product suite reflects this thinking.

items.title: USTR Proposes Extending China Ship Port Fee Suspension Through January 2027
items.original_title: USTR Proposes Extending China Ship Port Fee Suspension Through January 2027
items.summary: A cargo ship full of shipping containers is seen at the port of Oakland, California, U.S., August 4, 2025. REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year. For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue. USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels.

items.title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
items.original_title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
items.summary: By Yongchang Chin and Nathan Risser (Bloomberg) –US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million. Asian refinery orders for US crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels this month sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they weren’t authorized to publicly comment. If that pace of orders holds through the end of this month, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa. The tanker rate along the US Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost $60 million as of Thursday, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Those eye-watering rates doesn’t include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around $100 a barrel. Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending $30 to $35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out last year, Hawkins said.

items.title: Rare Russian Diesel Shipment Expected in Norfolk November 2, Ahead of Tanker Bound for New York
items.original_title: Rare Russian Diesel Shipment Expected in Norfolk November 2, Ahead of Tanker Bound for New York
items.summary: A tanker carrying Russian diesel is expected to arrive in Norfolk, Virginia, on November 2, potentially becoming the first such shipment to reach the United States in more than three years. The Vietnamese-flagged PVT Azura (IMO 9423683), reportedly carrying 109,000 barrels of Russian diesel, departed St. Petersburg on October 15 and is currently signaling Norfolk as its destination, according to VesselFinder . The arrival would come five days ahead of another Russian diesel shipment identified by Reuters on Friday as the first cargo heading to the United States under a recent agreement between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The tanker has signaled New York as its destination, with an expected arrival date of November 7, although its final discharge port has not been confirmed. The two shipments come as the Trump administration moves to ease restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. On October 9, Trump announced an agreement under which Russia would immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.

items.original_title: European gas caps strong weekly gain on Middle East supply escalation
items.summary: European wholesale natural gas prices surged on Friday, on course to cap the week at their highest levels since late 2022, as an escalation in Middle East military conflict and diplomatic evacuations intensified anxieties over global LNG supply continuity ahead of winter. The benchmark rose 3.8% on Friday to trade at 93.40 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh), locking in a weekly gain of nearly 7%. In Great Britain, the equivalent similarly advanced 3.5% to 229.00 pence per therm, on course to finish the week 6.2% higher. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis launched coordinated drone and missile strikes targeting civilian transport and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including a fatal strike on a civilian airport in Dammam and an attack on ’s Shaybah oilfield. The escalating conflict has severely restricted Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) carrier navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, forcing extended reroutings around Africa and drastically curtailing spot arrivals at European regasification terminals. Benchmark jumped to $114 per barrel on Friday – their highest level in over five months – reinforcing broad-based inflation and input cost pressures across energy-intensive European industries. The weekly surge across European gas curves leaves the continent acutely vulnerable as winter heating demand accelerates.

items.title: Singapore must look beyond the box to secure its logistics future
items.original_title: Singapore must look beyond the box to secure its logistics future
items.summary: Dropping behind Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan in the global container port rankings, and seeing Malaysia’s Port Klang and Port of Tanjung Pelepas nip at its heels should serve as a wake-up call for Singapore, in a changing competitive landscape for box trades For Singapore, this is about more than losing a place in a league table. It is an existential question asking whether a nation built on maritime trade can adapt to a world where supply chain control matters as much as moving containers. As Singapore spent years living off its geographical advantages, deepwater harbour and reputation for efficiency to guarantee continued dominance, its competitors have expanded their infrastructure, attracted manufacturing investment, and developed integrated logistics ecosystems. Part of the problem for Singapore with its nearest rival is that it simply cannot compete with Malaysia when it comes to land availability, meaning it should not focus on warehouses and distribution centres. And the pending Tuas Port, with its planned capacity of 65m teu on full completion in the 2040s, will have a part to play, even if success cannot be judged by volume alone. Yes, the Ministry of Transport’s new Connectivity & Logistics division recognises the need to integrate maritime, aviation, and land transport, but creating a coordinating body will not automatically deliver the commercial agility needed to compete.

items.title: Boxship orderbook bulges as race for giant vessels heats up
items.original_title: Boxship orderbook bulges as race for giant vessels heats up
items.summary: The container shipping orderbook has swelled to 46.5% of the active fleet, a post-2009 peak, as carriers race to secure ultra-large tonnage. With the orderbook at 16.2m teu, newbuilding activity shows no sign of slowing – Chinese shipyards alone have booked a record 4.94m teu this year, accounting for 88% of the total capacity ordered, according to Linerlytica. The orderbook-to-fleet ratio is also expected to grow, with Maersk and CMA CGM in the market for more giant ships. Tellingly, Hengli Heavy Industries announced today it had won orders for 52 ultra-large dual-fuel containerships: 20 of 24,000 teu; 20 ; of 19,000 teu; and a dozen of 22,000 teu. Maersk, which was dethroned from the top of the liner rankings in 2022 by MSC, is now eyeing a dozen 24,000 teu ships, up to 24 LNG dual-fuel 19,000 teu vessels and six at 18,600 teu. Zhonggu Logistics has entered the large ship segment, ordering a 14,000 teu pair at Hudong-Zhonghua for $155m each, joining fellow mid-sized shipping lines such as Emirates Shipping Line, Regional Container Lines, TS Linesm and China United Lines. Delivery is set for 2029 to 2030. On Tuesday, HMM announced it had ordered eight 13,000 teu LNG dual-fuelled ships from HD Hyundai Heavy Industries for around $1.5bn, for deployment on its Far East-India-Mediterranean service from 2029.

items.title: NSR vs Suez: the Arctic is not a tradelane, it’s a corridor with a hefty premium
items.original_title: NSR vs Suez: the Arctic is not a tradelane, it’s a corridor with a hefty premium
items.summary: On 19 October, data from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) showed 104 ships had crossed Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) by 30 September, already more than in all of 2025. Four days earlier, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported that containerships moved 2.19m teu through the Suez Canal last month, the most since the Houthi campaign began, and Linerlytica expects carriers to be fully back to Suez by the first quarter of 2027. Most coverage reads the first as proof that the Arctic is finally opening, but read together, they say something else: the part of the NSR Moscow planned and paid for has missed its targets by a wide margin, while the part it barely planned for has beaten them, because other people’s chokepoints closed. It isn’t that the NSR is missing from an Arctic section; the Arctic silk road itself is absent. Whatever the final figure, it is clear the season moved less than one 24,000 teu ship carries on a single Suez sailing. I costed the loop the way a carrier’s network team would: a 4,900 teu ship, eight seasonal sailings, west through the Arctic and back via Suez. The escort adds $150,000-$280,000 a transit, and Chinese sources put Arctic hull and P&I cover at three to five times normal rates.

items.title: South Korean Shipowner Sinokor Dominates Hormuz Transits as Oil Flows Rebound
items.original_title: South Korean Shipowner Sinokor Dominates Hormuz Transits as Oil Flows Rebound
items.summary: Oct 23, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A little-known South Korean shipowner dominated oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz in September, data from intelligence firms suggest, with the group’s vessels moving more barrels than the next three owners combined. Ships owned by Sinokor Group carried 105.6 million barrels of crude through the waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with global markets, an analysis of ship-tracking and other data from intelligence firms Vortexa, Equasis and Signal Group showed. That’s equivalent to almost 40% of oil making the crossing last month. of Saudi Arabia, also known as Bahri, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.’s shipping unit — accounted for a combined 97.3 million barrels during the same period, according to Bloomberg calculations based on that data. When Hormuz was all but closed off, those tankers were snapped up at exorbitant rates by producers who needed to load oil or risk running out of storage space and then being forced to undertake costly shutdowns. As Gulf crude exports recover to close to pre-war levels, Sinokor is still among the most active owners in the so-called shuttling trade, with its vessels taking short trips to pick up oil from inside the Persian Gulf, sail through Hormuz and then discharge at ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman.
